column4: The question مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ opens the fire-side confession in which the section's prayer, food, heedlessness, and denied account are gathered.
The answer "we were not among those who prayed" supplies the failed-prayer member of the confession opened in 74:42.
The confessors say that they did not feed the poor, reproducing the section's neglected miskīn as one cause of Sakar.
Their joining those who plunged into vain talk gives the confession its heedless immersion, corresponding to the section's missed heart in prayer; 74:43-46 specify the whole sequence.
وَكُنَّا نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ closes the confessed sequence with the same denial of the Day of Account that opens surah 107.
أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يَنْهَى repeats the section's demand to look and directs that look toward a person obstructing worship.
عَبْدًا إِذَا صَلَّى identifies what is being stopped: a servant in the act of prayer, making the path in 96:9 physically and spiritually interrupted.
The second أَرَأَيْتَ asks whether the praying servant is upon guidance, adding the half-blocked way named in the section to 96:9-10.
The possibility that the servant commands taqwā makes his interrupted prayer an inwardly directed act, unlike prayer performed for spectators.
أَرَأَيْتَ إِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى joins looking, denial, and bodily turning away in the very scene of obstructed prayer.
أَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرَى makes God's unbroken seeing the answer to worship arranged for human eyes.
يُدَعُّونَ إِلَى نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ دَعًّا uses the same d-ʿ-ʿ root as the source's violent pushing of the orphan, but the push now drives the denier into fire.
هَذِهِ النَّارُ الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ بِهَا تُكَذِّبُونَ explicitly identifies the fire toward which 52:13 pushes them as the fire they denied.
The woe pronounced on the deniers begins the short sequence that reaches pushing and fire in 52:13-14, matching the source's movement from denial to woe.
The deniers are immersed in playful خَوْض immediately before being pushed, a close counterpart to heedless immersion before reckoning; 52:13 gives its destination.
ثُمَّ الْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ supplies the fire sense carried by the section's ṣ-l-y/ṣ-l-w wordplay on "those who pray."
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ repeats the rare wording about not urging the feeding of the poor and gives the reason for 69:31's fire.
The condemned person has no close protector there, extending the source's broken protective circle around the vulnerable; 69:34 states his failure toward the poor.
His only food is foul discharge, a punitive reversal of the food he would not urge for the poor in 69:34 and of the household hearth developed in the section.
مَنُوعًا names the human being as intensely withholding when good reaches him, the same m-n-ʿ disposition embodied in withholding māʿūn.
إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ begins the explicit exception to the withholding person of 70:21 and opens the intact circle that surah 107 breaks.
Those excepted are constant in their prayer, directly reversing prayer from which the heart has wandered.
Their wealth contains a مَعْلُومٌ حَقٌّ, turning the withheld small due into an acknowledged and measured right.
The known right is for both the asker and the deprived, specifying the overlooked poor person who receives it.
They affirm the Day of Account, completing the exact reversal of denial, neglected prayer, and withheld property across 70:21-26.
The source's dictionary water sense of māʿūn meets مَعِين here, while آوَيْنَاهُمَا places Mary and her son in a secure resting place beside flowing water.
فِي غَمْرَةٍ سَاهُونَ is the other pointed Quranic use of the source's s-h-w root: heedlessness becomes an engulfing depth rather than mere distraction in prayer.
The heedless people of 51:11 ask when the Day of Account will be, joining their inattention to the reckoning denied in the section.
The answer places those heedless questioners over the fire for trial, continuing the section's move from sahw to fire.
They are told to taste the trial they sought to hasten, completing 51:11-13's heedlessness-account-fire sequence.
When hypocrites rise to prayer lazily, يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ and remember God only a little; prayer, the human gaze, and the absent heart coincide exactly.
The m-n-ʿ wording "nothing prevented" their spending from acceptance sits in one ayah with disbelief, lazy prayer, and unwilling expenditure, a dense parallel to the section's broken links.
Spending wealth رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ is joined to disbelief in God and the Last Day, so visible giving and denial of account occupy one act.
The giver who spends رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ while disbelieving in God and the Last Day makes charity into the same spectator-facing surface as the section's prayer.
كَلَّا بَل لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ gives the direct social failure toward the orphan whose continuation is failure to urge feeding in 89:18.
وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ closely repeats the section's rare urging-food construction immediately after neglect of the orphan.
Those who consume orphan property eat fire into their bellies and سَيَصْلَوْنَ سَعِيرًا, joining the orphan's withheld due to the fire-bearing prayer root.
فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّى pairs refusal to affirm with refusal to pray, setting up the denial and turning away in 75:32.
وَلَكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى repeats the denial-and-turning pair of 96:13 as the explanation of not praying in 75:31.
الَّذِي يَصْلَى النَّارَ الْكُبْرَى gives the fire side of the section's prayer/fire word meeting only three ayat before actual prayer.
The one in that fire neither dies nor lives, spelling out the endured consequence attached to the fire verb in 87:12.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى turns from the fire-bound person to purification, preparing the genuine prayer of 87:15 and recalling māʿūn as zakat.
وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى answers 87:12's fire-bearing form with remembered, God-directed prayer rather than prayer emptied of attention.
لَا يَصْلَاهَا إِلَّا الْأَشْقَى introduces fire with the same ṣ-l-y form that the section hears beneath the name of prayer.
The fire-bound person is الَّذِي كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى, reproducing denial and turning away before the passage contrasts him with a giver.
The Godfearing person gives his wealth to purify himself, reversing both withholding and spectator-facing devotion.
His gift is not repayment for a favor owed to anyone, clarifying that the giving is free of the social debt and gaze the section exposes.
إِلَّا ابْتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ الْأَعْلَى makes the Lord's face alone the aim of the giver in 92:18, the sharpest opposite of human-directed display.
كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِالدِّينِ repeats denial of dīn and immediately opens a scene of uninterrupted observation and recording.
وَإِنَّ عَلَيْكُمْ لَحَافِظِينَ places guardians continually over those who deny account, echoing the gaze that never leaves.
The guardians are noble scribes, converting unseen observation into the written account denied in 82:9.
يَعْلَمُونَ مَا تَفْعَلُونَ states that the observers know the deeds, including the small acts people overlook or perform for other eyes.
يَصْلَوْنَهَا يَوْمَ الدِّينِ puts the fire verb and the Day of Account in one line after 82:9-12's denial and surveillance.
وَمَا هُمْ عَنْهَا بِغَائِبِينَ says they cannot be absent from that fire, reversing the attempt to let the poor or one's own prayer fall out of sight.
وَيْلٌ لِلْمُطَفِّفِينَ moves the section's woe into the marketplace, where a small due is withheld rather than a small household aid.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from people, matching the section's people who insist that they themselves not be skipped.
When they measure for others they diminish the due, a transactional form of withholding māʿūn.
The question whether such people expect resurrection joins the apparently small withheld amount to accountability.
The resurrection is specified as a tremendous Day, enlarging the moral weight of the small shortage in 83:2-3.
People stand before the Lord on that Day, replacing the customers' gaze with the final divine accounting of the unequal exchange.
Another woe falls on the deniers, linking the commercial withholding of 83:1-3 to the source's denial-and-woe movement.
الَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ names the object of their denial as the Day of Account.
ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ لَصَالُوا الْجَحِيمِ gives the fire-bearing ṣ-l-y outcome of the denial named in 83:11.
The d-y-n wording shifts from judgment to literal debt: write a debt to its term and do not tire of recording it, whether small or large, so the source's account and small debt fully meet.
Immediately before the debt rule, a Day is feared when every soul returns to God and is paid in full, joining worldly obligation to final settlement.
A debtor in hardship must be given respite, and remission as charity is better; this states the mercy due at the small-debt end of the image.
The trusted person must discharge the trust entrusted to him and fear God, directly governing a borrowed household object when no written record is available.
قُلْ أَرَأَيْتُمْ asks the reader to look, then imagines water disappearing and asks who can bring مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ; sight, hidden provision, and the source's flowing-water sense converge.
A cup مِن مَعِينٍ brings a vessel and the source's flowing-water sense of māʿūn into one compact image.
أَكْوَابٍ وَأَبَارِيقَ وَكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ gathers cups, ewers, and flowing drink, directly staging the vessel-and-water meanings that the section places inside one word.
Golden dishes and cups are passed around while their contents delight the eyes, joining household vessels, circulation rather than withholding, and the image of sight.
مَنَّاعٍ لِلْخَيْرِ names the condemned person as an emphatic preventer of good, the same m-n-ʿ character embodied by withholding māʿūn.
مَنَّاعٍ لِلْخَيْرِ again fixes the tight-fisted character in the source's m-n-ʿ root, now within a portrait of public moral corruption.
The garden owners whisper that no poor person should enter upon them that day, turning overlooked need into a deliberate closed-door policy.
They set out early intent on withholding, making the refusal of the poor person's food an organized act; 68:24 states its target.
When commanded to spend from God's provision, the disbelievers ask whether they should feed someone God could feed, joining refusal of food to unbelief.
The transgressors' مَأْوَاهُمُ النَّارُ is a fire-abode from which they are returned whenever they try to leave, and they are told it is the fire they denied.
وَيَصْلَى سَعِيرًا begins a compact sequence in which fire, the household, denial of return, and God's seeing converge.
The fire-bound person had been joyful among his own household, bringing the home into the accountability sequence of 84:12-15.
He supposed he would never return, expressing the denial of final accounting beneath his ease at home.
إِنَّ رَبَّهُ كَانَ بِهِ بَصِيرًا answers that denial with the Lord's constant seeing, exactly as 96:14 answers performative prayer.
Their ṣalāt at the House is only whistling and clapping, and punishment answers their disbelief; it is another worship-form emptied of its inward act.
Successors who neglected prayer and followed desires will meet ruin, giving a direct outcome for prayer allowed to lapse.
The one who prevents God's name being mentioned in places of worship and strives to ruin them parallels the prayer-obstructor in 96:9-10 and receives disgrace and punishment.
When people see trade or diversion they rush toward it and leave the speaker standing; the eye abandons worship for visible provision while God's provision is declared better.
God knows the stealthy glance and what breasts conceal, joining the section's field of human looking to the inward heart that outward prayer misses.
The command to act is followed by the warning that God, His messenger, and believers will see the work before return to the Knower of hidden and visible, setting public gaze inside final accounting.
The restrained poor are thought rich because they do not beg insistently and must be recognized by their mark; they are precisely the faint, easily missed needy person in the section's visual field.
The frown and turning away bodily enact the section's skipped weak person and begin a sustained correction of misplaced attention.
The person passed over is blind, making the ethics of seeing and being unseen concrete.
The self-sufficient person is the one granted attention, corresponding to those who demand not to be passed over.
فَأَنتَ لَهُ تَصَدَّى says attention is actively directed toward the self-sufficient person, sharpening the unequal distribution of the gaze.
The other person comes striving, so his low visibility cannot be confused with lack of inward purpose.
فَأَنتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّى names distraction from that sincere seeker, closely paralleling the source's attention that skips the dim person and prayer's heart.
The command not to let one's eyes pass beyond sincere worshippers toward worldly adornment directly reverses overlooking the socially faint and following a heedless heart.
A man with weak offspring loses a rivered garden to a fiery whirlwind, bringing dependent children, water, provision, and fire into one warning scene.
The command to take a due charity and pray over the givers makes that prayer a tranquility for them, restoring the section's broken circle of share, prayer, and inward rest.
أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَآوَى answers the pushed orphan with God's finding and sheltering; its آوى also leads to the water-shelter meeting in 23:50.
Sincere worship, prayer, zakat, and دِينُ الْقَيِّمَة stand together here as the intact obedience whose pieces the section shows separated.
Righteousness is denied to a mere facing posture and defined through the Last Day, giving wealth to orphans and the needy, prayer, and zakat—the full positive structure behind the section's critique.
Prayer and zakat stand beside lending God a good loan, so the section's worship, due share, and debt image meet as willing obedience.
The covenant joins prayer, zakat, faithful support, and a good loan to God, an explicit repaired version of the section's prayer-and-debt relation.
People whom trade does not distract from remembrance, prayer, and zakat fear a Day when hearts and eyes overturn; inward attention, share, account, and sight remain joined.
Prayer and zakat are followed by the assurance that every good sent ahead is found with God and that God sees what people do, opposing worship for human eyes.
The command not to stretch one's eyes toward worldly display restrains the very gaze that misses the lowly; 20:132 redirects the household to prayer and divine provision.
Command the household to prayer and persist in it; God asks no provision but provides, joining home, sustained worship, and provision without display.
They feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, reversing both the pushed orphan and food withheld from the needy.
They feed solely for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, directly opposing an act arranged for spectators or social return.
Their fear of a harsh Day supplies the affirmed account behind the sincere feeding in 76:8-9.
Silver vessels and cups circulate as the reward of the sincere feeders, reversing the household vessel withheld as māʿūn.
The crystal-silver vessels are measured precisely, adding exact measure to the freely circulating household ware of 76:15.
فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ turns God's shelter in 93:6 into a command never to dominate or repel the orphan.
وَأَمَّا السَّائِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids rebuffing the asker at the door, the direct ethical reverse of denying small aid.
Feeding on a day of hunger is named as the hard ascent, turning the mouth that does not urge food into a costly act of provision.
The first recipient is an orphan of kin, joining feeding to restoration of the orphan's lost protective circle.
The second recipient is a needy person in dust, making visible the socially low person the source says is easily missed.
Open charity is allowed, but hidden charity to the poor is better; the ayah draws the boundary between visibility itself and spectator-seeking display.
Whatever wealth is spent seeking God's face returns fully to the giver, joining pure intention to repayment without wrong.
Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, show that visible giving need not be riyā when the act remains accountable to God.
Those seeking their Lord's face establish prayer and spend secretly and openly, and their reward is the final Home; gaze, prayer, provision, and dwelling are rejoined.
Believers are told to establish prayer and spend secretly and openly before a Day with no trade or friendship, placing both visible and hidden giving under account.
Those settled in the Home welcome migrants and prefer them despite their own need; the open dwelling and conquest of inner stinginess reverse the closed house of māʿūn.
Distribution is assigned to kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, turning the small withheld share into a protected social right.
The repaired wall protects treasure belonging to two orphan boys until maturity because their father was righteous, materially restoring the protective ring around orphan property.
The command to give orphans their property and not consume it makes the orphan's due inviolable rather than something a stronger hand may push aside.
Guardians must test orphans, deliver their property, avoid consuming it, and call witnesses; وَكَفَى بِاللَّهِ حَسِيبًا joins protection of the due to divine accounting.
When orphans and the needy attend a division, they are to receive something and hear kind words, a direct refusal to let the faint person at the edge leave empty-handed.
Guardians are told to imagine leaving weak offspring behind, fear for them, and speak rightly, articulating the protective circle the source's orphan lacks.
Setting orphan affairs right is declared best, and sharing life with them makes them brothers; household inclusion answers expulsion at the door.
Do not drive away those who call their Lord seeking His face; their account is not yours and yours is not theirs, joining sincere worship, refusal to repel, and separate accountability.
People of means must not swear to stop giving kin, the needy, and emigrants, a direct prohibition on turning grievance into withheld aid.
A due for the asker and deprived is present in their wealth, the compact counterpart of 70:24-25 and the opposite of withholding the small share.
Obligatory alms are assigned to the poor, needy, debtors, and other named recipients, joining māʿūn's zakat sense to its debt image through protected shares.
The command to hear, obey, and spend is paired with deliverance from the soul's stinginess, opposing the hand that withholds māʿūn.
A good loan to God follows the command to spend and is multiplied and forgiven, converting the debt image into willing generosity.
The successful believers are inwardly humble in prayer, supplying the heart-attention missing from the section's outward prayer.
The same portrait makes them active in zakat, keeping prayer and the due share joined.
They guard trusts and covenants, a direct ethic for the borrowed object that māʿūn can denote; 23:9 then returns to prayer.
They carefully guard their prayers, closing the trust-and-prayer sequence with the opposite of sahw.
Within the same Meʿāric portrait, the worshippers guard trusts and covenants, extending the known financial right to borrowed or entrusted things.
They guard their prayers, closing the longer sequence begun with constancy in prayer and containing the known right and affirmed account.
The intoxicated may not approach prayer until they know what they are saying, defining conscious speech as a boundary against prayer whose heart is absent.
أَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِذِكْرِي states remembrance as prayer's purpose, the direct inward answer to being heedless of one's prayer.
A flowing spring in the garden reverses the punitive spring of 88:5 and supplies the water side of the section's māʿūn image.
Cups are set ready beside that garden scene, bringing available vessels together with flowing water rather than withholding them.
Large basins and fixed cauldrons are made for David's household, followed by "work in gratitude"; the source's dictionary pot sense becomes an implement of grateful service.
No mountain can shelter Noah's son from the flood: his attempted refuge and overwhelming water form the failed boundary opposite the secure high resting place and flowing water of 23:50.
Faces enter a blazing fire with the ṣ-l-y verb; the following ayat turn immediately to drink and food, making this a compact fire-hearth reversal.
They drink from a boiling spring, a punitive joining of water and the fire scene in 88:4 rather than the sheltering flowing water of 23:50.
They have no food except a thorny plant that neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, the negative endpoint of refusing food to the needy.
The town refuses the travelers hospitality, yet a collapsing wall is repaired there; 18:82 reveals that the wall shelters orphan property.
The garden owners are introduced as a test case of people planning a harvest; 68:24-25 disclose that their plan is to exclude the poor.
A visitation destroys the garden while they sleep, making hidden judgment answer the hidden plan to withhold the poor person's food.
Those who hoard wealth and do not spend it in God's way are warned of painful punishment, joining closed wealth to the fire detailed in 9:35.
The hoarded metal is heated in hell and brands bodies, turning withheld wealth into the fire it has earned.
The water-drawer lowers his bucket into the well, giving a concrete Quranic scene for the source's dictionary sense of māʿūn as a bucket, though the narrative is rescue rather than lending.
At the water of Midian, two women hold their flock back while others draw, staging vulnerable people waiting at access to water.
Moses waters for the two women without demanding return, a small act of water-aid that reverses withholding māʿūn.
Permission to eat from relatives' and friends' houses portrays household food and access as socially shared, a broad but concrete opposite to the closed shelf and door.
The record leaves neither small nor large uncounted and presents every deed, making the section's smallest withheld aid part of the denied account.
Everything people have done is in written records, corresponding to the account that outward display cannot evade.
Every small and great thing is inscribed, giving the smallness of māʿūn full weight within that account.
Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock or anywhere else is brought by God, a nonvisual parallel to the faint person and small deed that human sight misses.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, joining the smallest helpful act to eventual seeing and account.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, ensuring that even a tiny refusal hidden behind public prayer is not missed.
The just scales for Resurrection allow no wrong, and even a mustard-seed weight is brought forward, linking precise repayment to the small due.
God sheltered a small, vulnerable people, strengthened them, and provided good things; the awā root joins protection and provision as in the orphan and Mary scenes.
Those who gave shelter and help become mutual protectors, extending the source's shelter verb into a human protective circle.
The army leaves home boastfully and رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ, extending the source's spectator-facing conduct from prayer and charity to a public procession.

The source's Suhā-star example makes Abraham's seeing a star and then observing it set a plausible visual echo: a star is attended to rather than missed, though this ayah does not concern prayer or aid.
After the deniers are pushed to the fire they denied, the question whether it is magic or they cannot see adds the section's seeing motif to that exact push-fire scene.
The person sent to fire did not believe in God; this ayah supplies the denial immediately before 69:34 identifies his failure to urge feeding the poor.
Those who affirm the Day in 70:26 also fear their Lord's punishment, showing the inward force that keeps prayer and the poor person's known right intact.
The Day of Account culminates when no soul controls anything for another and command belongs to God, defining the final settlement behind 82:9-18.
The record of the wicked is introduced immediately after the short measure and resurrection scene, making the small withheld due a written matter of account.
The question asking what can convey the nature of Sijjīn interrupts complacent vision and directs attention to the record named around it.
A written register completes 83:7-8, corresponding to the accounting that captures the small shortage of 83:2-3.
The deniers are veiled from their Lord before entering fire in 83:16, turning the section's seeing-and-being-seen field into a punitive loss of sight or access.
The question asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, a direct divine-scale counterpart to the human hand that withholds a small provided good.
One covenant joins worship of God, kindness to orphans and the needy, good speech, prayer, and zakat, gathering nearly every link whose dissolution the section traces.
Worship of God is joined to good treatment of orphans, the needy, near and distant neighbours, and travelers; 4:37-38 then expose withholding and display as violations of this command.
The stingy both command others to stinginess and conceal God's bounty, the precise negative counterpart to urging food and making provision available.
Those who refuse zakat are identified in the same ayah as disbelievers in the Hereafter, directly joining the withheld due to denial of account.
The question whether these lowly worshippers are really the ones God favored exposes the social gaze behind driving them away; 6:52 states their sincere worship and separate account.
The overlooked blind visitor may purify himself, showing the inward value missed by the gaze that turns toward the self-sufficient.
He may receive a reminder that benefits him, specifying what is lost when attention skips him.
The addressee is not accountable for the self-sufficient person's refusal to purify himself, undercutting the impulse to give that person preferential attention.
The overlooked seeker comes in fear, adding inward reverence to the striving named in 80:8 before he is neglected in 80:10.
The garden owners realize that they themselves have been deprived, a pointed reversal of their plan in 68:24-25 to deprive the poor person.
Some who are called to spend withhold, but their stinginess is against themselves; the ayah explicitly turns refused provision back upon the withholder.
The Godfearing person is kept away from the fire before 92:18 describes his purifying gift, completing the passage's reversal of denial, turning away, and fire.
Prayer, zakat, and certainty in the Hereafter form one positive triad, the intact opposite of heedless prayer, withheld māʿūn, and denial of dīn.
The same prayer-zakat-certainty triad recurs as the identifying practice of those who do good, reinforcing the section's linked rather than separated obedience.
The God-conscious establish prayer and spend from provision, while 2:4 completes their portrait with certainty in the Hereafter.
Certainty in the Hereafter supplies the account-facing stance for the prayer and spending named in 2:3.
A good loan to God is multiplied, and God constricts and expands provision before return to Him; debt, provision, and final repayment meet directly.
Charitable men and women are described as lending God a good loan that is multiplied, converting the section's withheld small debt into freely offered aid.
The command to return trusts to their owners gives the direct ethical rule for a borrowed household item and places its return under just judgment.
Those who gave shelter and help are declared true believers, repeating the awā shelter formulation as a human protective circle around the vulnerable.
The ruling concerning orphan women and oppressed children commands that justice be upheld for orphans, making visible the dependents whom stronger household members could overlook.
Do not approach orphan property except in the best way until maturity, and give full measure and justice; the orphan's protection and the small due meet in one command.
Protection of orphan property until maturity is joined to fulfilling the covenant because covenants are questioned, placing guardianship under account.
Giving kin, the needy, and the traveler their due states the positive obligation corresponding to the share withheld as māʿūn.
Giving kin, the needy, and the traveler their due is tied to seeking God's face, uniting the protected share with intention free of human display.
A fixed share of acquired wealth is assigned to kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers, preventing the vulnerable recipients from disappearing at distribution.
The concrete image of a hand chained to the neck marks the boundary of stinginess, while the warning against total extension keeps giving responsible.
Prayer and spending secretly and openly are joined to hope for a transaction that never fails, opposing display and withheld provision under a lasting account.
Those who spend seeking God's pleasure and inward certainty are compared to a fruitful garden, the intention-level opposite of the show-giver in 2:264.
Hell is brought forth on the Day in the same surah that has condemned failure toward the orphan and failure to urge feeding the poor, supplying their eventual fire horizon.
Those stingy with God's bounty will have what they withheld made a collar on Resurrection, turning the closed hand into a visible bond at account.
Wealth and children must not distract believers from remembrance; this gives a specific worldly form to the absent attention that the section finds in prayer.
The next command is to spend before death makes the person plead for delay to give charity, joining distraction to aid withheld until too late.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, giving the mouth at the needy person's door a positive role even when material aid is absent.
Woe opens a portrait of public contempt and accumulated wealth that ends with fire reaching inward hearts, echoing the section's woe and surface-versus-heart concern.
The condemned person amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it, a concrete closed-store counterpart to the small share or object that should circulate.
The accumulated-wealth portrait reaches God's kindled fire, joining hoarding to the fire consequence developed in the section.
That fire rises over the hearts, turning the inward center neglected in outward worship into the point reached by judgment.
